title: Lambdas and Higher-Order Functions
oneLiner: Functions as values: lambdas, Func and Action versus Python callables, passing functions in (sorting with key functions, map and filter), returning functions, closures, and the loop-variable trap.
keyTakeaway: A function is a value: store it, pass it, return it. A lambda is a short inline function, x => x * 2 or lambda x: x * 2. A closure captures variables, not their values, so lambdas made in a loop all see the loop variable's final value unless you copy it (C#) or bind it as a default argument (Python).
explanation:
This is the first lesson of the intermediate track. It assumes the basics track: variables, loops, functions, collections and classes in both languages.

In both C# and Python, a function is a value like a number or a string. You can keep one in a variable, put it in a list, pass it to another function, or have a function build and return a new one. A lambda is a small function written inline without a name, which is the usual way to hand a bit of behaviour to another function: "sort by this", "keep the items where this is true", "call this when the button is pressed". In C# the type of such a value is a delegate, normally one of the ready-made Func and Action types; Python simply calls anything callable.

A function that takes or returns another function is a higher-order function. Sorting with a key function, LINQ's Where and Select, Python's map, filter, sorted, min and max are all higher-order functions, and so is any function of yours that takes a test or a callback as a parameter.

A function created inside another function can use the outer function's variables, even after the outer function has returned. That function plus the variables it keeps alive is a closure. Closures are how a returned function remembers its settings, and they explain the classic bug where lambdas created in a loop all report the same value.
